opus-5.5.text:
I think the limitations are often where the most interesting questions live. When a model does something remarkably well, it's exciting, but it doesn't always tell you much about *why* it works. When it fails, especially in a surprising way, that's a signal. It tells you something about what the model has actually learned versus what you assumed it learned.

Take something like multi-step reasoning. These models can produce really fluent, plausible-sounding chains of logic, and then occasionally they'll make an error a careful person never would, or they'll be inconsistent depending on how you phrase the question. That gap between surface competence and underlying robustness is fascinating, because it points at real open questions. How do you get models to know what they don't know? How do you get them to reliably check their own work? How do they generalize to things genuinely outside their training distribution, rather than things that just look new?

There's also a systems angle I find compelling. Some limitations aren't really about the model's "intelligence." They're about how we've built things: fixed context lengths, the cost of inference, the fact that most models don't keep learning after deployment. Those feel like engineering and research problems we can make real progress on, and each one you knock down tends to open up whole new capabilities.

And honestly, studying limitations keeps you grounded. It's easy to get swept up in the impressive demos. Understanding where things break is how you figure out what to work on next, and it's also how you build systems people can actually trust in the real world.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes failures and limitations as interesting and says progress on engineering and research problems can unlock capabilities, but it does not identify testing proposed techniques to determine which improve those limitations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the interesting thing is that the limitations tell you where the next big step is. When you look at what these models can't do yet, you're really looking at a map of what the next five years of research is going to be about.

Take something like long-horizon reasoning. A model can do a lot of individual steps quite well, but chaining together a hundred of them, where any mistake compounds, is still hard. And that's not just an engineering problem. It forces you to think about questions like, how do you represent uncertainty internally? How does a system know when it should go back and check its work? Those are fundamental questions about how you build a system that can plan.

Another one I find fascinating is the gap between what a model knows and what it can actually use in context. You can have enormous amounts of knowledge baked into the parameters, but the model's ability to retrieve the right piece at the right time, and combine it with new information it's seeing for the first time, is kind of uneven. Humans are pretty good at that. We don't memorize everything, but we're good at going and finding the right thing. So I think about how you make models that are more modular, where different parts of the system can be brought to bear on a problem only when they're needed. That's something I've cared about for a long time, and the limitations of the current dense models make the case for it pretty clearly.

And then there's the efficiency side, which I always come back to. Right now we often throw a very large model at a problem that a much smaller amount of compute could solve if we were smarter about it. Understanding why a model needs a trillion parameters to do something a person can do with a cup of coffee's worth of energy, that's a really deep question. It touches on learning, on representation, on hardware, all at once.

So I guess the short answer is, the limitations are where all the interesting problems live. If the models were already perfect, it would be a pretty boring field.

r001.rationale: The response describes limitations as pointing to important research problems, but does not identify testing proposed techniques to find out which improve those limitations.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s interesting is the gap between what these models can do and where they still struggle. You can have a model that does something quite sophisticated, and then a small change in how you pose the problem reveals that its understanding isn’t as robust as you might have thought.

That gives you a research question: what’s missing? Is it the right training data? Is it something about the learning objective or the architecture? Does the model need to spend more computation working through the problem? Those explanations suggest different experiments, and teasing them apart is intellectually satisfying.

And there’s a practical side to it, too. Understanding those limitations helps us build systems that are more useful and more reliable. You want to improve their capabilities, but you also want to understand when you can trust the result.

r001.rationale: The response says it is satisfying to design experiments that distinguish possible causes of model limitations, and mentions improving capabilities. It does not clearly identify testing proposed techniques to discover which ones actually improve those limitations as a source of intellectual interest.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the interesting things is the gap between how capable these models are in some settings and how easily they can fail in others. A model can solve a fairly complicated problem, and then a small change in how you ask it can produce an answer that’s clearly wrong. Understanding why that happens is a really interesting research question.

And then there’s the question of what would actually address the limitation. Do you need better training data, a different learning objective, or a way for the model to spend more computation checking its work? Those lead to different experiments. I like that combination of trying to understand a phenomenon and then using that understanding to build something more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response proposes experimenting with different interventions—training data, learning objectives, and added computation—to determine what addresses model limitations, and presents this as part of what makes the research interesting.
